reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO & national toxicology guidance
clinicalPearls: A widely used grain fumigant that reacts with moisture and gastric acid to liberate phosphine gas, a potent mitochondrial poison, and is a common agent of fatal deliberate self-harm in some regions
There is no specific antidote, so management is entirely supportive and directed at aggressive haemodynamic and metabolic resuscitation
Profound, often refractory circulatory shock from direct myocardial toxicity and vasodilatation is the dominant and most lethal feature
Severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, myocarditis, arrhythmias, and multi-organ failure develop early
A garlicky or decaying-fish odour on the breath or vomitus is a clinical clue to phosphine exposure
Rescuers must be protected, as phosphine off-gassed from vomitus and gastric contents can poison staff; ventilate the area and avoid mouth-to-mouth

Reported adjuncts include gastric decontamination with agents intended to reduce phosphine liberation, magnesium, high-dose steroids, intravenous lipid emulsion, and vasopressors, though evidence is limited
Early intensive-care support with vasopressors, correction of acidosis, and consideration of extracorporeal circulatory support offers the best chance in a highly lethal poisoning
reference.pathophysiology: On contact with water or gastric acid, aluminium phosphide releases phosphine gas, which inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase and generates reactive oxygen species, arresting oxidative phosphorylation across tissues. The heart is especially vulnerable, developing myocardial depression, myocarditis, and arrhythmias, while widespread vasodilatation and cellular energy failure produce profound refractory shock. Lipid peroxidation and oxidative injury drive a severe metabolic (lactic) acidosis and multi-organ dysfunction affecting the liver, kidneys, and adrenal glands.
additionalInvestigations: Continuous ECG and cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia and myocarditis
Arterial blood gas with anion gap and lactate
Serum electrolytes including magnesium, renal and liver function
Silver nitrate paper test on breath or gastric aspirate to detect phosphine where available
redFlags: Refractory hypotension and shock unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors
Severe metabolic acidosis with rising lactate
Arrhythmias or echocardiographic evidence of myocardial dysfunction
Large ingestion of a fresh (unexposed) tablet, associated with very high mortality
Risk of secondary poisoning of healthcare staff from off-gassing
reference.prognosis: Poisoning carries very high mortality, particularly with fresh tablets and established shock or severe acidosis; death commonly occurs within the first day or two from cardiovascular collapse, and survival is largely determined by ingested dose and speed of intensive supportive care.
pitfalls: Expecting a specific antidote to exist and delaying aggressive supportive resuscitation
Underestimating lethality because the patient initially looks stable before rapid deterioration
Neglecting staff protection against phosphine off-gassing from the patient
Inadequate correction of acidosis and under-resuscitation of shock
